text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- The position of the Bank of Finland cannot be determined with a simple majority vote, parliament constitutional committee says, opposing the government.
- Finance Ministers Arja Alho and Sauli Niinisto in dispute over stamp duty on bank loans which Alho wants to abolish but Niinisto does not.
- Euro-minister Ole Norrback -- chairman of the Swedish People's Party -- has been a cabinet minister for 10 years without interruption.
- The European Commission will probe shipping firm Finnlines' deal with the City of Helsinki to swap land.
- A group of environmental activist protesting against cutting trees in old forests tried to stop a shipment of Finnish paper near Amsterdam.
- All reindeer passed doping tests in a race in Lapland.
KAUPPALEHTI
- The forecast fall in unemployment this year would boost the state finances by 3.5 billion to four billion markka, says labour ministry special planner Eero Polus.
- Finance Minister Sauli Niinist rejects idea of referendum on joining EMU.
AAMULEHTI

- The military service system may be changed already next year, cutting the shortest possible time of service to six months from eight but upping the longest to 12 from 11 months, army headquarters says.

- The Baltic Sea region is Europe's most promising and economically expansive area and it is a home market area which Finland and Sweden can benefit from, said Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson on a brief visit in Finland.

- Over half of the members of the Condeferation of Unions for Academic Professionals in Finland (Akava) are prepared to take a turn leave to create more jobs, but fear of losing jobs and lost income caps enthusiasm.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Finns use cashpoint machines more than other Europeans, survey shows.
DEMARI
- Supreme Court judges should not be allowed to rule in courts of arbitration, says social democrat MP Markku Pohjola.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET

- Computers will soon be able to understand the concept of 'almost', says Iranian-born professor Lotfi Zadeh, an expert in the field of artificial intelligence and so called soft computing, on a visit to Finland.
